title: Shohei Ohtani’s return to the mound is imminent. How will the Dodgers manage him?
content:
LOS ANGELES — Shohei Ohtani could return to the mound for the Los Angeles Dodgers even sooner than expected.

Ohtani threw a 30-pitch live session against Will Smith on Saturday, his first time facing hitters since his last big-league pitching appearance on July 3, as he’s dealt with nagging knee trouble. On Sunday, manager Dave Roberts left open the possibility that Saturday’s session could be the last box to check before Ohtani pitches for the Dodgers again.

The Dodgers do not have a set starter for Sunday’s series finale against the Detroit Tigers. Ohtani starting that game and throwing one inning is an option the club is considering, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the club’s thinking who cannot comment publicly because those plans are not finalized. Previously, there had not been a timeline for Ohtani other than vague assurances he would be back this season.

Ohtani’s status will depend on how he feels in the coming days and after his next bullpen session, slated for this week while the team is in Atlanta.

“I think it’s more of how the pen goes,” Roberts said Sunday morning, acknowledging that Ohtani’s return could be near.

The Dodgers have shifted Eric Lauer into a relief role for at least this next turn through the rotation. The left-hander said Sunday morning he could provide length as soon as Tuesday or Wednesday with Tyler Glasnow (making his first start since May) and Roki Sasaki as probable starters. If Ohtani does pitch, Lauer would be the logical piggyback option, Roberts acknowledged.

Ohtani has battled left knee discomfort since June, and the Dodgers pushed pause on his pitching a month later. He missed the All-Star Game to receive a “lubricant” injection in that knee. Ohtani has had at least three incidents of right biceps discomfort, the last of which caused the Dodgers to slow down his pitching ramp-up.

It interrupted a special season on the mound that could have warranted consideration for his first Cy Young Award. Ohtani has made 14 starts, logging 85 2/3 innings with a 1.79 ERA. His 228 ERA+ ranks third in the majors among pitchers with at least 85 innings.

Roberts said this weekend that Ohtani’s health issues are “behind us,” and Ohtani’s play as a designated hitter has reflected that. He has been more aggressive on the basepaths and more apt to push it with his legs in recent weeks as he has pursued another MVP award.

The Dodgers were methodical with how they built up Ohtani in a similar situation last summer. When Ohtani returned from his second major elbow surgery last June, they repeated his one-inning increments before moving to the next stage. The Dodgers are operating with less time this go-around, and will be “a little bit more aggressive” with how they move Ohtani’s workload up each start.

Ohtani could still build up to five-inning starts by October, Roberts said. If Ohtani keeps his standard once-per-week pitching schedule, he could get up to four or five (if he starts Sunday, with the regular season ending Sept. 27) starts in actual games before then.

“To then have the opportunity, the flexibility to insert Shohei to build up like he did last year, I think, is of huge benefit both ways,” Roberts said.

Even if he is not a full-fledged starter in October, the Dodgers would benefit massively from having Ohtani as a pitching option. He would have to start whatever game he pitches in to maximize the Ohtani rule, but having him essentially serve as an opener would give the Dodgers fewer innings to cover with their 13 other pitchers in the postseason.

It is also an added luxury for a club whose postseason starting options include, among others, a World Series MVP (Yoshinobu Yamamoto), two multi-time Cy Young Award winners (Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell) and the club’s 2024 Opening Day starter and All-Star (Glasnow).
